title: Ticket folder layout
ask: How are artifacts organised in the knowledge repo?
why: The folder shape every ticket uses. Agents, the validator and ticket pages all depend on it.
learn: lc-wms layout 3, control-center artifacts, paperclip llm-wiki
rec_reason: One folder per ticket with state in TOML and prose in markdown is the shape both of your repos converged on.

options.label: Folder per ticket: ticket.toml + flat markdown
options.desc: lc-wms layout 3: state in TOML, docs as {T}-spec.md, {T}-plan.md and so on, plus a wiki/ area for durable notes.
pros: Everything about a ticket in one place
Easy to validate with a layout spec
Maps to a generated ticket page
cons: Many small files
Moving a ticket means moving a folder
options.pick_if: tickets carry several artifacts each.

options.label: Flat markdown with YAML frontmatter
options.desc: Simplest, but state in frontmatter is easy to corrupt.
pros: Simplest to start
cons: State in frontmatter is easy to corrupt
No clean place for trackers
options.pick_if: tickets are just notes.

options.label: Wiki-style raw/ and wiki/ only
options.desc: Good for notes, weak for delivery workflow.
pros: Good for durable notes
cons: No delivery workflow, trackers or gates
options.pick_if: this is only a notebook.

title: Artifact types
ask: What lives in the knowledge center?
why: The set of artifacts the system must create, validate and display.
learn: lc-wms, control-center

options.label: Spec / requirements (BR, AC)
options.desc: One spec edited in place; decisions table inside.

options.label: Plan + tasks
Test cases
Graphs and diagrams
Decision log
options.desc: What was chosen, why, what was rejected.

options.label: Questions and bugs trackers
Daily work logs
Wiki / durable notes
Templates
options.desc: Starting files for every artifact kind.

options.label: Investigations (no ticket)
options.desc: Triage dossiers before a ticket exists.

options.label: Release notes

decided.note: Your saved picks (plan-picks.json). Diagrams live inside spec and plan markdown, not as a separate artifact type.

title: Finding things
ask: How do you and the assistant search the knowledge base?

options.label: Ripgrep + a generated artifact map
Add embeddings later
options.desc: Semantic search once the corpus grows.

options.label: Browse only

why: No database: search is ripgrep plus a generated JSON index, and Obsidian search over the markdown.

decided.note: Ripgrep plus a generated index. No embeddings in v1.

title: Stages (board lanes)
ask: What is the lifecycle of a ticket?
why: Lifecycle lanes drive the board, the pipeline gates and every agent scope. Lanes come from the workflow plugin (F46); this card picks the default pack.
learn: lc-wms board-ticket.toml, paperclip statuses
rec_reason: Six lanes cover the real pipeline (requirements, plan, build, verify) without the release lane you do not need yet. Blocked is a flag, not a lane.

options.label: backlog > spec > plan > build > verify > done, plus a blocked flag
options.desc: Lite version of lc-wms lanes, blocked is a flag not a lane.
pros: Maps one-to-one to agents and gates
Small enough to see on a board
cons: No release lane until you add one
options.pick_if: you want a clear delivery pipeline.

options.label: lc-wms: backlog, requirements, planning, build, verify, release, done (+parked)
pros: Includes release and parked
Proven in lc-wms
cons: Release handling is out of scope for lite
options.pick_if: you ship releases through the same board.

options.label: paperclip: backlog, todo, in_progress, in_review, done, blocked, cancelled
options.desc: Generic task statuses; no spec/plan stages.
pros: Generic and familiar statuses
cons: No spec or plan stages, so agents lose their lanes
options.pick_if: you only track tasks, not delivery.

options.label: todo, doing, done
options.desc: Very light; loses the delivery pipeline.
pros: Dead simple
cons: Loses the whole pipeline
Gates have nowhere to attach
options.pick_if: never for a delivery system.

decided.note: Default pack: backlog, spec, plan, build, verify, done. Blocked is a flag, not a lane. No release lane in v1.

title: Ticket IDs
ask: How are tickets named?
learn: lc-wms, paperclip (PAP-12)

options.label: Local sequential: T-001, T-002
Prefix per project: WMS-12, APP-4
Adopt an external tracker key (Jira, Projexa)

why: Ids appear in file names, links and commit messages; changing them later is painful.

decided.note: Readable counter. F61 adds an author or random suffix so two branches cannot mint the same id. Consistency fix (B24, 2026-10-07): Superseded in format by F61: T-014-sa.

title: Ticket fields
ask: What does a ticket carry?

options.label: Title, summary, stage, blocked flag
Size S/M/L
Priority
Owner (human or agent)
Repo, branch and artifact links
Labels
Parent / sub-tickets
Estimate and actual hours
Due date
Goal or project link (why this ticket exists)
options.desc: Paperclip ancestry: tickets roll up to goals.

why: Fields drive the board, filters and agent decisions, and each one is another thing to keep valid.

decided.note: Core fields plus a project and goal link, so agents receive why the ticket exists (F94).

title: Per-ticket trackers
ask: Which TOML trackers sit inside each ticket?
learn: lc-wms has five; two overlap

options.label: Questions
options.desc: Open questions with blockers exit code.

options.label: Bugs
Todos
Gaps
Critique findings

why: Trackers are the gates: open questions or bugs stop a ticket moving on.

decided.note: Questions, bugs and todos. Gaps and critique findings can be added when those skills need them.

title: Ownership and claiming
ask: How do you stop two agents doing the same ticket?
learn: paperclip atomic checkout

options.label: Atomic claim with conflict error (never retry)
options.desc: claimed_by and claimed_at; second claimer gets a 409-style refusal.

options.label: No claiming (single user, one agent at a time)
options.desc: Simplest; breaks when you run agents in parallel.

decided.note: One claimer. A second claim is refused and not retried. Consistency fix (B24, 2026-10-07): Atomic on one machine; a duplicate claim across branches is caught by hl validate on merge.

title: External tracker sync
ask: Do tickets sync with anything outside?

options.label: None in v1
options.desc: Local is the source of truth.

options.label: GitHub issues
Jira / Projexa push

decided.note: The knowledge repo is the source of truth in v1.

title: Model
ask: How do todos and tasks relate?
why: How chores and plan work relate; affects capture speed and traceability.
learn: control-center todos, lc-wms tasks.toml
rec_reason: Todos stay light and never block; plan tasks carry acceptance-criteria links. Keeping them separate keeps both simple.

options.label: Two things: todos (light, optional ticket) and tasks (plan tasks with AC links)
options.desc: Todos never block. Tasks belong to a plan and trace to ACs.
pros: Light capture
Plan tasks stay traceable
cons: Two concepts to explain
options.pick_if: you want quick capture and strict planning.

options.label: One unified item with an optional ticket and plan slot
pros: One list
cons: More fields on every item
Blurs chores and plan work
options.pick_if: you want a single backlog.

options.label: Todos only
pros: Simplest
cons: No plan-level tracing
options.pick_if: no formal planning.

decided.note: Todos stay light and never block. Plan tasks carry acceptance-criteria links.

title: Todo features
ask: What can a todo do?

options.label: General inbox (not tied to a ticket)
Ticket-scoped, movable in and out
options.desc: Promote a todo into a ticket.

options.label: Priority and due date
Capture from Telegram and voice
Checklists
Recurring and reminders

decided.note: No recurring todos: there is no scheduler in v1 (F18).

title: Work log format
ask: Work is logged as one file per person per day in the knowledge repo, as in lc-wms and control-center (kept). Which line format?
learn: lc-wms logs/YYYY-MM/YYYY-MM-DD.author.toml; control-center the same path as markdown with ## Work bullets

options.label: TOML entries per person per day (lc-wms): ticket, category, text, weight, hours
options.desc: Structured and queryable, easy for the Work tab.
pros: Totals, weights and timesheets are easy
Tool validates every entry
Never conflicts in git (one file per person per day)
cons: Not visible in Obsidian unless notes are generated (F52)
options.pick_if: you need timesheets or per-ticket totals.
options.must: Decided rule: TOML for structure, one file per person per day.

options.label: Markdown bullets per person per day (control-center): author in frontmatter, ## Work lines
options.desc: Easy to read; harder to aggregate.
pros: Native in Obsidian and any editor
Simplest to read
cons: Hours and weights are text to parse
Easy to hand-edit into inconsistency
options.pick_if: the log is for reading, not totals.

options.label: Append-only activity JSONL
options.desc: Paperclip-style audit log of everything; great for dashboards, noisy for humans.
pros: Append-safe for machine events
cons: Poor for a human timesheet
Mixes intent with audit noise (that is F70)
options.pick_if: you only want an event stream.

why: The log feeds the work view, timesheets and standup digests. One file per person per day also means two people never conflict in git.
rec_reason: Structured entries let the console total hours and weights and build timesheets. Obsidian sees the markdown notes the console generates (F52); control-center style markdown is the readable alternative.

decided.note: One TOML file per person per day. The console generates the readable note.

title: How entries get created
ask: Who writes the log?

options.label: /log-work skill and console quick-add
Automatic from agent runs (Stop hook)
options.desc: Run summary appended when an agent finishes.

options.label: Telegram /log
Automatic on ticket moves

why: Who writes the log. Agent runs are attributed to the person who ran them, with no agent names in the text.

decided.note: A person, a finished agent run, or a stage change. No separate Telegram log command. Consistency fix (B24, 2026-10-07): The Stop hook is the only automatic log for runs; the do skill does not log again. Second review (B25, 2026-10-07): Ticket moves go to the activity log, not the work log.

title: Reports
ask: What do you read back?

options.label: Work tab: today and yesterday
Timesheet by ticket
options.desc: Hours per ticket per day (lc-wms had at least 8h/day).

options.label: Weekly summary
Standup digest

decided.note: Today and yesterday first. Timesheet and standup can be generated later from the same file.

title: Ids that survive branches and teams
ask: How are ticket and record ids created when several people work on branches?
why: Two people creating T-014 on different branches collide at merge.
rec_reason: A sequential counter is easy to read but collides across branches. A short per-author or random suffix avoids collisions at a small readability cost.

options.label: Short unique ids: a counter plus the author's initials, for example T-014-sa
pros: No merge collisions
Still short enough to type
cons: Less pretty than T-014
Gaps in numbering
options.pick_if: two or more people create tickets on branches.

options.label: Plain sequential counter (T-001, T-002) stored in one file
pros: Easy to read and say aloud
cons: Merge conflict on the counter file
Duplicate ids across branches
options.pick_if: a single person, one branch.

options.label: Time-ordered random ids (ULID)
pros: Globally unique, sortable
cons: Long and ugly for humans
Needs a friendly alias on top
options.pick_if: ids are mostly machine-referenced.

decided.note: Assumed: several people edit on branches, so ids must not collide.

title: Record granularity: one file per record or per kind
ask: Do decisions, questions and bugs live as many entries in one file or one file each?
why: Teams editing the same ticket on different branches merge cleanly only if they touch different files.
rec_reason: One file per record makes git merges and Obsidian notes line up one-to-one, at the cost of more files. Combine both: records are files, a generated index lists them.

options.label: One file per record (decisions/D-003-sa.toml, same author suffix as tickets, F61) plus a generated index
pros: Two people editing different records never conflict
Maps one-to-one to an Obsidian note
Easy history per record
cons: Many small files
Listing needs the index or a directory scan
options.pick_if: a team shares the knowledge repo.

options.label: One file per kind per ticket (decisions.toml with many entries)
pros: Few files
Easy to read as a whole
cons: Same-place appends conflict in git
Harder to link to one entry
options.pick_if: a single person works on each ticket.

options.label: Per kind for small kinds (tasks), per record for those that attract concurrent edits (decisions, bugs)
pros: Fewer files where conflicts are rare
cons: Two rules to remember
options.pick_if: you want a middle path.

decided.note: One file per record so two people can edit the same ticket on different branches. Spec and plan stay flat at the ticket root (F2a).

title: How structured records show up in Obsidian
ask: Obsidian only graphs markdown notes. How do TOML records appear in the knowledge graph?
why: Decides whether decisions, bugs and tasks are visible, linked and searchable in Obsidian, or invisible.
learn: Obsidian core: links, backlinks, graph, Properties (YAML frontmatter), Bases; Dataview community plugin
rec_reason: Keep TOML as the source (safe to write) and generate readable markdown notes from it. The generated notes carry wikilinks and YAML properties, which are what Obsidian understands. Generated files may use YAML frontmatter because Obsidian requires it.

options.label: Generated markdown notes: a verb writes hub notes for each ticket and each record, with wikilinks and properties; the TOML stays the source
pros: Records join the graph, backlinks and search
Source stays TOML (safe to write)
Notes are read-only views, so nobody edits the wrong copy
cons: Generated notes must be kept fresh (events, git hook)
Duplicated information on disk
options.pick_if: you want Obsidian to be a real window on the whole knowledge base.
options.must: Decided rule: Obsidian only graphs markdown, so a verb writes notes from the TOML.

options.label: Records are markdown with YAML properties, one file per record (Obsidian-native); no TOML for records
pros: Native in Obsidian, Dataview and Bases
One file, two audiences
cons: Needs a YAML-frontmatter parser and writer dependency
Hand edits can corrupt state
Reverses the TOML decision (F24)
options.pick_if: Obsidian is the primary editor for everyone.

options.label: Obsidian shows only authored markdown (spec, plan, notes, wiki); records stay invisible to it
pros: Nothing to build
cons: Decisions, bugs and tasks are missing from the graph
options.pick_if: Obsidian is only for reading prose.

decided.note: TOML stays the source. A verb writes the markdown notes Obsidian graphs. Consistency fix (B24, 2026-10-07): Notes are not in git (F129); hl notes (or the session-start hook) builds them locally from the shared TOML.

title: Obsidian vault setup
ask: Is the knowledge repo itself an Obsidian vault, and what ships in it?
why: Teams need the same graph, templates and exclusions without sharing personal layout.
learn: Obsidian ignores folders starting with a dot; .obsidian holds shared config and per-user state

options.label: The scaffold commits a minimal .obsidian (graph colours per artifact kind, templates folder, excluded folders, core plugins on) and gitignores per-user state (workspace.json)
pros: Same graph groups and templates for the whole team
Generated HTML and logs stay out of the graph
cons: Shared config can clash with personal taste
options.pick_if: a team uses the vault.

options.label: No .obsidian in the repo; each person configures their own
pros: No config to maintain
cons: Everyone has a different graph; no shared templates
options.pick_if: only you use Obsidian.

options.label: Also ship community plugins (Dataview, Templater)
pros: Queries and rich templates
cons: Plugins must be installed and trusted by every user
Fragile across versions
options.pick_if: you want dashboards inside Obsidian.

decided.note: A minimal .obsidian ships with the vault. Core features only. No Dataview or other community plugins.

title: What blocked means
ask: Can a ticket just be marked blocked, or must it say why and who acts?
why: Paperclip requires a named owner and next action for blocked; a prose-only "blocked" hides stuck work.
learn: paperclip execution semantics
rec_reason: Blocked is a flag with required fields: blocked_by (a ticket, question or person) and next_action. The inbox and dashboard show these first.

options.label: Blocked requires blocked_by and next_action; the validator refuses a bare flag
A plain blocked flag

decided.note: Blocked needs blocked_by and next_action. A bare flag is invalid.

title: Audit trail
ask: Is every state change recorded as who did what, when?
why: Paperclip logs every action with actor and entity. The work log (F6) is human intent; an audit trail is every verb call. It powers the dashboard feed and "who changed this".

options.label: Every verb call appends a line to an activity JSONL, one file per person per day (like the work log): actor (agent or person), verb, entity, time, result and the person on whose behalf it ran
Rely on git history

decided.note: Every verb appends one JSONL line. The work log stays the human timesheet. Second review (B25, 2026-10-07): Activity is committed (one file per person per day).

title: Work log rules
ask: Which rules keep the work log trustworthy? These come from lc-wms log-work, which you already use.
learn: lc-wms log-work: the tool owns storage, author, dedupe and hours; control-center logs

options.label: The tool owns storage, author, file layout, duplicate detection (about 70% similar text on the same day is skipped) and hour allocation; you supply one sentence
One plain sentence, up to about 160 characters, no agent or skill names: the log is a timesheet for people
Weight 1 to 5 as a share of the day; hours only for a fixed block such as a meeting; day length override
Categories: Development, Code Review, Testing, Design, Documentation, Internal
Special tickets for meetings and leave, kept out of delivery tickets
Author comes from the people roster, never guessed, one file per author per day
options.must: Decided rule: the author is read from the roster, never guessed.

why: A timesheet nobody trusts is worse than none. These rules, proven in lc-wms, keep entries short, unique and attributed.

decided.note: The tool owns the file. The author comes from the roster and is never guessed.

title: Goal context for agents
ask: Do agents see why a ticket exists, not just its title?
why: Paperclip links tasks to projects and goals so agents receive the goal behind their work. A one-line why changes what an agent builds.
learn: paperclip README: Goal Alignment, goal-aware execution
rec_reason: Keep it light: a ticket links to a project and a goal (a short markdown note). The context digest includes that chain, so agents get the why for free.

options.label: Ticket links to a project and a goal; `hl context` includes the goal chain in the digest
options.desc: The why travels with the work.

options.label: A free-text "why" field on the ticket only
Titles and specs only

decided.note: A ticket points at its project and goal. hl context includes that chain.

title: Ticket thread and run history
ask: Where do comments, plans, blockers and agent run history live relative to the ticket?
why: Paperclip task threads keep conversation, plans, blockers, files and run history attached to the work. Today our plan has comments only as a verb; there is no thread or run list on the ticket page.
learn: paperclip README: Task Threads; control-center ticket comments tracker
rec_reason: A comments record per ticket for the human conversation, plus a run record per agent run (who, what, result, usage) listed on the ticket page. Both are files, so they travel with the ticket.

options.label: Per-ticket comment records (author, time, text) and per-run records (agent, start, end, result, usage, transcript link) shown as Thread and Runs tabs on the ticket page
options.desc: Everything about the work in one place.

options.label: Comments only
No thread; discuss in chat or git

decided.note: A ticket thread and a run list. Comments on a spec passage stay in git review (F100), not a second store. Second review (B25, 2026-10-07): Comments and run records are committed; transcripts and audio stay on the machine.

title: Slicing model and vocabulary
ask: How is a ticket broken into work? What do we call the pieces: phase, slice, layer, task, wave?
why: The words decide how plans, tasks.toml, agents and the board talk to each other. Mixed vocabulary is how plans end up with 60 tasks and no shippable increment.
learn: lc-wms plan: slices S1..Sn, tasks S1-T1, layers db|api|ui|test|env|spike|docs, waves for parallel dispatch; control-center breakdown-tasks: phases, slices, tasks with ids like 2-3-2; control-center idea doc: layer-as-phase
rec_reason: lc-wms uses the model that works: a slice is a thin vertical cut that delivers at least one acceptance criterion end to end; a task is one layer. Phase is a pipeline stage, wave is parallel dispatch, and neither is a way to slice. control-center T-017 grew to 4 phases, 10 slices and about 60 tasks, which shows why.

options.label: Ticket, then slices, then tasks. A slice is a thin vertical cut through every layer it needs, delivering at least one acceptance criterion end to end, riskiest first, testable on its own. A task belongs to exactly one layer (db, api, ui, test, env, spike, docs; the list is configurable). One slice for size S, two to five for M and L, more than six means split the ticket. Phase means a pipeline stage and wave means parallel dispatch; neither slices work
pros: Every slice can be shipped and verified alone
Risk is retired first
Tasks map to one layer, one owner, one test
Plans stay small enough to read
cons: Needs discipline to keep slices vertical
Cross-slice dependencies must be stated
options.pick_if: you want plans that deliver working increments.

options.label: Phases, then slices, then tasks (control-center implementation-plan template), task ids like 2-3-2
pros: Familiar project-plan shape
Room for very large tickets
cons: Layer-as-phase means nothing works until the last phase lands (lc-wms rejects it)
One real ticket reached about 60 tasks
Three-part ids are hard to read
options.pick_if: tickets are program-sized.

options.label: A flat list of up to six tasks per ticket, no slices
pros: Fastest for small tickets
cons: No structure for medium and large work
No definition of done per increment
options.pick_if: every ticket is small.

decided.note: A slice delivers one acceptance criterion end to end. A task is one layer. Phase is a pipeline stage.

title: Ticket folder structure
ask: What folders and files does a ticket get? Where do SQL scripts, rollback scripts, plans, decisions, trackers, tests and source material go?
why: This is what the scaffold creates and the validator checks. Agents, the console and Obsidian all rely on it. Blueprint 16 has the full tree with a reason per entry.
learn: lc-wms ticket-layout.toml (layout 3) and real tickets WLC-973, WLC-975; control-center flat _template of 13 files; both repos
rec_reason: Keep what works in lc-wms (data-driven layout, lazy folders, source and test-cases dirs) and fix its rough edges: one spelling for release folders, visible forward and rollback pairs, trackers as per-record files (F62), prefixed unique file names (F26).

options.label: Flat root with a few lazy subfolders: ticket.toml, spec, plan, tasks.toml; decisions, questions, bugs and gaps folders of one TOML file per record; architecture/, db/ (forward, rollback, dev, README), test-cases/, tests/, source/, investigations/. Lazy: a folder exists only when it holds a file
pros: Everything for a ticket in one place with a clear home for each thing
Forward and rollback SQL are visible as pairs
Merge-friendly per-record files
Matches what you have already refined
cons: A migration path from lc-wms tickets
More folders than the flat control-center layout
options.pick_if: tickets carry SQL, tests and several trackers.

options.label: lc-wms layout 3 as it is: ticket-scripts/{development-scripts, handy-scripts, reference-scripts, release-scripts/{created-or-altered, inserts-or-deletes, rollback-scripts}}
pros: Already in use and validated by your tooling
cons: Deep nesting; three spellings of the insert and delete folder across skills
Pairing of forward and rollback is not enforced
The inserts folder is not staged (a known pitfall)
options.pick_if: you want zero change from today.

options.label: control-center flat layout: {T}-{artifact}.md files at the root, scripts in ticket-scripts/
pros: Few folders
cons: No home for SQL pairs, tests and evidence
Grows into 20+ flat files
options.pick_if: tickets are small and have no SQL.

decided.note: New tickets use this tree. Existing lc-wms tickets keep their folders until an optional migrate. The validator reads the layout version from ticket.toml. Consistency fix (B24, 2026-10-07): ticket.toml and tasks.toml keep fixed names; markdown files carry the ticket prefix (F26).

title: Database scripts and rollback
ask: Where do SQL scripts and rollback scripts live, how are they named and ordered, and what approves them?
why: SQL is the riskiest thing a ticket ships. lc-wms already has hard stops for it; the structure should make pairing and order checkable by a program.
learn: lc-wms database-operations, prepare-release-sql, stage-release, plan schema gate; tickets WLC-973, WLC-975, WLC-980
rec_reason: One numbering rule does three jobs: sort order is run order, the same number pairs a rollback with its forward script, and a validator can check it. Drop the type folders and the inserts folder that cause staging pitfalls.

options.label: db/forward/NN_{schema}.{object}.sql and db/rollback/NN_{schema}.{object}.rollback.sql with the same NN; sort is run order; db/dev/ for throwaway diagnostics; db/README.md lists catalog order and rollback order; DML goes in forward with a preview flag; multi-catalog tickets use numbered folders; schema changes need an approved question before slices; the validator warns on an unpaired script
pros: Pairs are obvious and machine-checkable
No ordering bugs from type folders
DML cannot be forgotten by staging
Rollback order is documented where the scripts are
cons: Differs from lc-wms folder habits
Staging tooling must read the new layout
options.pick_if: you want safe, reviewable database changes.
options.must: Requested: SQL forward and rollback scripts with the same number in the ticket.

options.label: lc-wms nesting: created-or-altered/[type]/ and rollback-scripts/, with a separate inserts-or-deletes folder
pros: Matches your release skills now
cons: Pairing not enforced
Rollback naming suffix is not matched by the validator
inserts-or-deletes is not copied by staging
options.pick_if: you will keep the existing release skills unchanged.

options.label: SQL lives only in the project repo migrations; the ticket links to it
pros: One place for scripts
cons: The ticket is no longer a self-contained package
Review needs the project branch
options.pick_if: the project has a strong migration tool of its own.

decided.note: Same number pairs a forward script with its rollback. Release packaging (run-all, rollback-all, DEPLOY.md) stays a workspace or project skill, not in the system layer. Second review (B25, 2026-10-07): These SQL rules ship in the software-delivery pack (F141), not the system ticket model.

title: Test artifacts
ask: Where do test cases and executable checks live?
why: lc-wms keeps test-case documents in the ticket but real tests in product repos, which works; ticket-local scripts need a home too.
learn: lc-wms test-cases with TC-U/I/E/N/B/X ids traced to AC; generate-e2e-tests writes into a separate test repo

options.label: test-cases/ in the ticket (TC ids traced to AC, reports, evidence/); product tests live in the project repo; ticket-local executable checks (SQL, Python, shell) in tests/, linked from the test cases; every PASS shows the command and output
Everything including product tests in the ticket
All tests in the project; the ticket only references them

decided.note: Test-case documents live in the ticket. Product tests live in the project repo.

title: Shared knowledge across projects
ask: Every knowledge center has information that belongs to every project. Where does it live, and what about things that are useful but not skills?
why: Standards, glossary, environment notes, runbooks, SQL snippets, contracts and the team roster are used by many tickets and projects. Today lc-wms spreads them across wiki, data-graph, _shared artifacts and skills.
learn: lc-wms wiki, data-graph catalog (projects.toml, glossary, status-codes, fk-map), _shared/common-handy-scripts, templates/checklists; control-center wiki
rec_reason: One shared area at the root of the knowledge repo for cross-project reference, one folder per project for project-specific notes (the overlay from F87), artifacts per ticket and logs per person. Skills stay procedures and link to shared reference instead of embedding it.

options.label: A shared/ area (wiki with standards, decisions, runbooks, environments, glossary; sql snippets and diagnostics; templates; checklists; contracts and data dictionaries; people and special tickets) plus projects/<id>/ for per-project notes and the overlay (F87), artifacts/ per ticket, logs/ per person
pros: Each kind of knowledge has an obvious home
Agents find reference through one index, not by loading it
Skills stay small
cons: Folders to explain
Existing wiki notes must be sorted into them
options.pick_if: several projects share conventions and data.

options.label: One flat wiki with tags
pros: One place
cons: Reference and per-project notes mix
Hard to apply per-project rules
options.pick_if: a single project.

options.label: Reference lives inside skills (lc-wms today for SQL rules and verify scopes)
pros: Always next to the procedure
cons: Loaded as skill text, costing tokens
Duplicated across skills
Invisible to people and Obsidian
options.pick_if: a handful of tiny rules.

title: Reference versus skill
ask: When is something a skill and when is it reference?
why: A clear rule keeps skills small and reference findable. The wrong choice either wastes tokens or hides knowledge.
rec_reason: A skill is a procedure the agent executes. Reference is a fact the agent looks up. Reference is never loaded automatically; skills link to it, and a generated index (one line per shared document) lets agents and people find it.

options.label: A skill is a procedure; reference is a fact. Reference is never auto-loaded: a generated shared/INDEX.md lists each document in one line, hl search finds it, and skills link to it instead of embedding it
options.must: Requested: reference material that is useful but is not a skill.

options.label: Embed standards in the skills that use them
Put standards in CLAUDE.md

title: Lifecycle tiers: what archiving and deleting mean
ask: As tickets pile up, too many files confuse the LLM. What happens to a ticket after it closes?
why: Without a lifecycle the knowledge base only grows, search gets noisy and agents read stale material. lc-wms and control-center only flag stale and archive on the board; neither has a real archive or a delete.
learn: lc-wms close-ticket and board archive flag (nothing deleted); control-center close-work archive step (skill text only) and reset (dry run, typed confirmation); deepseek-harness archived/manifest with sha256 and a value test before deleting; paperclip 7/30/90-day retention and reopen cooldown
rec_reason: Four tiers. Active tickets stay small. Closing writes a digest and hides drafts. After a retention window the ticket moves to a restorable archive with a hash manifest. Deletion is allowed only for archived tickets, after a value check, with a tombstone left behind.

options.label: Four tiers: Active (capped file count, a keep pin, stale is only a flag); Closed (a closure digest, drafts moved to a hidden _work/); Archived (moved to archive/YYYY-MM/T-xxx with ticket.toml, the digest and a sha256 manifest; restorable); Deleted (purge with a dry run, typed confirmation, a value check and a tombstone)
pros: Active work stays small and readable
Archiving is reversible: restore verifies the hashes
Deleting is possible, but only with safeguards and a record
Matches the patterns in all four repos
cons: More verbs and states to learn
Digests must actually be written well
options.pick_if: the workspace will grow past a few dozen tickets.

options.label: Two tiers: active and archived; nothing is ever deleted (lc-wms today: an archived flag on the board)
pros: Nothing is lost
Least code
cons: Files keep accumulating
The LLM still sees them unless hidden
No way to remove information that should not be kept
options.pick_if: storage and noise are not a concern yet.

options.label: Remove closed tickets from the tree; git history is the archive
pros: The working tree stays small
No archive structure to maintain
cons: Hard to find or restore (git archaeology)
Search and Obsidian lose the context
deepseek-harness rejects history as the only copy
options.pick_if: git is the only record you trust.

decided.note: Active, closed (digest), archived (restorable), deleted (only after a dry run and a typed confirmation).

title: The closure digest
ask: What stays readable after a ticket closes, so the full folder can be hidden or archived?
why: A short, fixed-shape summary lets people and agents learn what a ticket did without reading 20 files. It is the compaction of information.
learn: lc-wms closure_summary on the graph node; deepseek-harness 8-section compaction checkpoint (merge, do not copy; (none) for empty sections); control-center context digest (about 16 times fewer tokens)
rec_reason: A fixed-section digest of about 400 words: outcome, decisions with their reasons, key files and links, caveats, follow-ups, each saying (none) when empty. The close skill writes it and a verb checks the shape and size. It stays in the working tree and in Obsidian after the rest is archived.

options.label: A fixed-section closure digest of up to about 400 words (outcome, decisions with reasons, key files and links, caveats, follow-ups); the close skill drafts it, a verb validates shape and size; it stays in the tree and the Obsidian graph
pros: Anyone can learn what happened in a minute
Uniform shape is easy for agents to parse
Lasting rationale survives deletion of the rest
cons: Someone (or the agent) must write it well at close
A bad digest hides detail
options.pick_if: tickets close faster than people re-read them.

options.label: A free-text summary line
pros: No template
cons: Too thin to replace the folder
Inconsistent
options.pick_if: tickets are small.

options.label: No digest; keep or archive the whole folder
pros: Zero effort
cons: Archived tickets cannot be understood without opening everything
Deleting loses the story
options.pick_if: you never delete.

decided.note: About 400 words: outcome, decisions, key files, caveats, follow-ups. Consistency fix (B24, 2026-10-07): On archive, the digest note is written to shared/digests/ so the graph keeps it.

title: Keeping old material out of the LLM context
ask: How do we make sure agents and search do not read closed and archived files by accident?
why: deepseek-harness hides its archive with a single ignore line; lc-wms hides nothing and its index still lists closed items; control-center caps its digest at 1,200 characters. Hiding is the part that actually protects the model.
rec_reason: Layer the protections: hidden folders, host deny rules, search and context defaults that cover only hot tickets, and size caps on every digest the agent loads at session start.

options.label: Layers: _work/ and archive/ in the ignore files for search tools and in host deny rules (Claude Read deny, Cursor Read deny); hl search and hl context cover active and capped closed digests by default, with --archived to include the rest; the session-start digest and the generated index are capped (about 12 rows or 1,200 characters); Obsidian excludes the archive folder
pros: Agents never wander into old files by accident
Search stays sharp as the workspace grows
Explicit access still works when you ask for it
cons: Several config files to keep in sync (generated from one source)
options.pick_if: you expect hundreds of tickets.

options.label: Search and context defaults only; no ignore files
pros: Little config
cons: Agents can still list and read archived folders directly
Editor search shows everything
options.pick_if: few tickets.

options.label: No hiding
pros: No effort
cons: The problem you described: too many files confuse the LLM
options.pick_if: never.

decided.note: Archive and drafts are hidden from search and from host read rules. Agents load digests, not old folders. Consistency fix (B24, 2026-10-07): Archived digests stay visible through shared/digests/.

title: Retention triggers and thresholds
ask: When does a ticket move from closed to archived, and when may it be deleted?
why: Thresholds should be settings, not code, and nothing should be deleted by a timer.
learn: lc-wms stale_days 14 and control-center 7 (flag only); deepseek-harness archive by judgement, not age; paperclip idle auto-archive after 90 days, deletion needs a person, reopen cooldown 7 days
rec_reason: Archive is suggested by age (for example 30 days after close) and done by a verb with a dry run. Deleting is never automatic: eligible after a longer window (for example 180 days) and always confirmed. A keep pin overrides everything. All numbers live in workspace.toml.

options.label: [retention] in workspace.toml (stale days, archive after, purge eligible after, keep pin); the session-start digest suggests what is eligible ("12 tickets can be archived"); archive and purge are verbs with a dry run; nothing deletes by itself
Archive automatically after the window; deletion still manual
No thresholds; archive when someone remembers

decided.note: Starting point: suggest archive 30 days after close, purge-eligible after 180. Nothing deletes itself. A new link restores the digest only.

title: Deleting tickets and information safely
ask: You want the option to delete tickets and information. What safeguards make that acceptable?
why: Deletion is the one irreversible step. lc-wms has no delete verb at all; control-center only has reset with a dry run and typed confirmation; paperclip hard deletes inside a transaction and leaves an audit entry; deepseek-harness leaves no trace, so inbound links must be repaired by hand.
rec_reason: Purge only archived tickets (or give a reason to override), show a dry run, require a typed confirmation, check the value first (move lasting rationale to the shared wiki or decision log), check inbound links, keep a tombstone record, and offer a short trash window. The same rules apply to other information kinds.

options.label: hl purge: only archived tickets (override needs a reason); dry run first; typed confirmation; a value check that promotes lasting decisions to shared/wiki/decisions; inbound link check (refuse or repair); a tombstone line (id, title, closed, deleted, reason, digest, hash) appended to archive/tombstones.jsonl; an optional trash window of N days; one audit line. The same verbs for other kinds: hl delete note, decision, log
pros: Deletion is possible and recorded
Lessons are not lost with the folder
References never dangle silently
A mistake can be undone inside the trash window
cons: Several steps for something rare
Tombstones and the trash folder to maintain
options.pick_if: you want to remove information with confidence.

options.label: A plain delete verb with a confirm prompt
pros: Simple
cons: No value check, no record, broken links
Easy to regret
options.pick_if: a throwaway workspace.

options.label: Never delete; archive only
pros: Nothing is lost
cons: You asked for deletion
Information that must go (wrong, sensitive) stays
options.pick_if: compliance requires keeping everything.

decided.note: Purge only an archived ticket, after a dry run, a typed confirmation, a value check and a tombstone. Later (after v1, B25): purge and tombstones; archive is in v1.

title: Compacting logs, chats and generated files
ask: Tickets are not the only things that grow. How do we compact the rest?
learn: deepseek-harness compaction checkpoints, spill-to-file with preview, tiered retention; paperclip tiered backups; lc-wms logs archived by month

options.label: Rotate JSONL history (chat, usage, audit, events) monthly and compress old months with gzip (gzip is built into Node; zstd later if wanted)
Roll usage and audit lines up into daily aggregates and keep the raw lines compressed
Summarise old chats into a fixed-section checkpoint (primary request, files, pending work, next step, critical context) and keep the raw log compressed
Leave daily work logs alone; add a monthly summary note and move old months to a logs archive
Generated pages and notes are never stored in git; they are rebuilt on demand
Large tool or agent output is spilled to a file with a short preview and a pointer, then swept after about 30 days
Size budgets with warnings: files per active ticket, evidence size, digest length, index rows

why: Logs, chats and generated files grow faster than tickets. Compact them early and the knowledge base stays fast and readable.

decided.note: Generated HTML is written for people and not committed. Agents read the source files. Consistency fix (B24, 2026-10-07): Obsidian notes are rebuilt locally by hl notes. Second review (B25, 2026-10-07): Rotation and gzip apply only to local files (chats, usage, transcripts); committed files are never gzipped. Later (after v1, B25): chat checkpoints and usage roll-ups.

title: A project as the unit of knowledge
ask: Each knowledge center holds several projects, and each project keeps its own knowledge, graphs and nodes. What is inside a project?
why: Paperclip projects own tasks, goals and workspaces; yours should also own the knowledge about the thing being built, so an agent working on a project finds everything in one folder.
learn: paperclip projects and project workspaces; lc-wms data-graph catalog and per-project registry; control-center wiki; Blueprint 22
rec_reason: One folder per project in the knowledge center: a project.toml (id, owners, code repos, goals, status), a hub note, a wiki for architecture, runbooks and environments, a graph of nodes, and an optional CLAUDE.md and skills overlay. Tickets link to the project id.

options.label: projects/<id>/ with project.toml (owners, code repos by .code-workspace folder name, goals, status), a hub note, wiki (architecture, runbooks, environments, project decisions, glossary), nodes/ (the project graph, F140) and an optional CLAUDE.md and .claude overlay (F87); tickets reference the project id
options.desc: Everything about a project in one place.
pros: An agent working on a project loads one folder, not the whole workspace
Project knowledge survives tickets and people
Matches the project layer of CLAUDE.md and skills (F86)
cons: More structure to keep tidy
Cross-project facts must go to shared/ deliberately
options.pick_if: a workspace holds more than one project.

facts.Holds: project.toml, hub note, wiki, graph, overlay

options.must: Decided rule: a project is the unit of knowledge, one folder per project.

options.label: Projects are only rows in workspace.toml; all knowledge lives in shared/
pros: Fewer folders
cons: Project knowledge mixes with everyone else
No natural home for project graphs
options.pick_if: projects are tiny.

options.label: Each project keeps its knowledge in its own code repo
pros: Knowledge is next to the code
cons: Other teams own some repos
Breaks the single knowledge center per team
Hard to graph across projects
options.pick_if: you own every repo.

decided.note: projects/<id>/ holds project.toml, a hub note, a wiki, nodes/ and an optional overlay.

title: The project knowledge graph
ask: Each project keeps graphs and nodes about what it is built from. How rich is the graph, and who keeps it current?
why: A graph lets an agent find the right five nodes instead of reading the project. lc-wms has a powerful one that drifted, so the shape and upkeep rules matter more than the depth.
learn: lc-wms data-graph (186 files, typed edges, agent index, LLM-maintained, drifted); control-center Vault graph (wikilinks and containment, typed edges dropped); paperclip llm-wiki (raw and wiki, index, log, contradiction flags); Blueprint 22
rec_reason: Keep typed edges (the part that makes impact analysis possible) but fix what drifted: outgoing edges only with computed inverses, one generator that writes the graph, index and lint report, a closed type set, and an agent contract that cites ids and marks unknowns UNVERIFIED. No catalogs that duplicate nodes, no confidence scores, no Obsidian CLI dependency.

options.label: Typed node notes in files: projects/<id>/nodes/<type>/<id>.md with frontmatter (id, type, title, summary, updated, sources, typed outgoing edges depends_on, part_of, touches, supersedes, see_also); outgoing edges only, inverses computed; one generator in the core package writes graph.json, a capped index.generated.md and a lint report; agents read the index, pick up to 5 nodes, follow up to 2 hops and cite ids; missing facts are marked UNVERIFIED and logged
pros: Impact analysis and "what touches X" are possible
Nothing duplicated by hand: inverses, indexes and lint are generated
Plain markdown, so Obsidian shows it natively
Agents load about 5 nodes instead of the project
cons: Someone or an agent must write the nodes and keep sources linked
A small generator to build
options.pick_if: projects have structure worth querying (systems, data, flows).

facts.Upkeep: Nodes by agents and people; everything else generated
facts.Agent cost: Index (about 150 rows) plus up to 5 nodes

options.must: Decided rule: typed markdown nodes, outgoing edges only, generated inverses, index and lint.

options.label: Links only: the graph is the markdown wikilinks between notes (control-center and Obsidian style), no typed edges
pros: No schema, nothing to maintain
Obsidian already draws it
cons: No typed queries or impact analysis
Agents cannot navigate by relationship
options.pick_if: notes are mostly prose and you only want browsing.

options.label: The lc-wms style data graph: LLM- and hand-maintained nodes with catalogs, stored inverse edges, confidence scores, ticket nodes, Dataview dashboards
pros: Detailed blast-radius reports for database work
cons: It drifted: README claims 458 tables against 310 indexed, inverse edges on 43 of 91 tables, a "generated" index edited by hand with zero edge counts
Heavy upkeep and an Obsidian CLI dependency
No measurement that it saves tokens
options.pick_if: you maintain a very large database estate and fund the upkeep.

facts.Agent cost: Index of about 4k tokens plus nodes

options.label: Add embeddings and graph retrieval on top (Graph RAG)
pros: Finds related material without exact links
cons: A vector index is a database in disguise, against your files-only rule
Heavy, and needs a model
Later, if search becomes the bottleneck
options.pick_if: the corpus is too large for index and grep.

decided.note: Closed types: component, concept, decision, data, flow, integration. Edges: depends_on, part_of, touches, supersedes, see_also. Database objects link to the source path and do not mirror columns. Later (after v1, B25): the project graph.
